Getting the Most Out of Your Muscles

  • For many endurance athletes, the rate at which oxygen (O2) is provided to working muscles is the limiting factor in their performance.
  • Your aerobic capacity is
    • the maximum rate at which O2 can be taken in and used by your muscle cells and
    • the most strenuous exercise that your body can maintain aerobically.
  • If you work even harder and exceed your aerobic capacity,
    • the demand for oxygen in your muscles will outstrip your body’s ability to deliver it,
    • metabolism then becomes anaerobic, and
    • your muscle cells switch to an “emergency mode” in which they
      • break down glucose very inefficiently and
      • produce lactic acid as a by-product.

Energy Flow and Chemical Cycling in the Biosphere

Chemical Cycling between Photosynthesis and Cellular Respiration

Text description of this image

The details of the flow diagram are as follows:

Sunlight energy enters an ecosystem and is used in the chloroplasts in plants during photosynthesis, a reaction that converts light energy to chemical energy.; The products of photosynthesis are the chemicals glucose (C6H12O6) plus oxygen (O2), which are in turn used in the mitochondria of both animals and plants for cellular respiration, a reaction that harvests food energy to produce ATP.; ATP is the form of energy that drives cellular work.; Heat energy converted during cellular respiration exits the ecosystem, completing energy’s one-way flow through the ecosystem.; The chemical products of cellular respiration, carbon dioxide (C O 2) plus water (H2O) remain within the ecosystem, and are in turn used by plants along with energy from the sun during photosynthesis.

Cellular Respiration: Aerobic Harvest of Food Energy

Text description of this image

An illustration shows a running woman inhaling O2, which enters the lungs and then travels to the body cells. Cellular respiration occurs in the muscle cells using O2, and the C O 2 produced is sent to the lungs, from where it is exhaled.

Overview of Cellular Respiration

The many chemical reactions that make up cellular respiration can be grouped into three main stages:

  1. glycolysis,
  2. the citric acid cycle, and
  3. electron transport.
Text description of this image

Cellular respiration occurs in both plant and animal cells.

The first step, glycolysis, takes place in the cytoplasm and converts glucose to two molecules of pyruvic acid while producing a small amount of ATP. High-energy electrons are also carried from this step to the final step via carrier molecules.; The second step, the citric acid cycle, takes place within the mitochondrion, and uses the products from glycolysis to produce a small amount of ATP. More high-energy electrons are also sent via carrier molecules to the final step.; The electron transport chain, the final step of cellular respiration, takes place across the inner membrane of the mitochondrion using the high-energy electrons from glycolysis and the citric acid cycle. This step produces a large amount of ATP.

Text description of this image

An equation shows glucose (C6H12O6) plus 6 O2 going through many chemical steps resulting in 6 C O 2 plus 6 H2O plus approximately 32 ATP molecules plus heat.

Glycolysis

Text description of this image

The details of the input, numbered steps, and output depicted in the figure are as follows: Input: Glucose, a six-carbon molecule. Step 1: During the energy investment phase, 2 ATP go to 2 ADP as glucose is split into two three-carbon molecules, each of which is attached to a phosphate group from the 2 ATP invested. The energy harvest phase consists of steps 2 and 3. Step 2: Each 3-carbon molecule then gains a second phosphate group as each donates a pair of electrons to NAD plus, forming NADH. Two total molecules of NADH are formed, one for each 3-carbon molecule split from glucose. Step 3: After several chemical steps, 2 ADP go to 2 ATP for each of the two 3-carbon molecules, with the removal of both phosphates that had been attached to each. The result is the formation of 4 ATP molecules in total. Output: Two 3-carbon molecules of pyruvic acid.

From Glycolysis to Citric Acid Cycle

Text description of this image

The details of the input, steps, and the output depicted in the figure are as follows: Input (from glycolysis): Pyruvic acid (a 3-carbon molecule). Step 1: Pyruvic acid loses a carbon as C O 2 and becomes acetic acid, a 2-carbon molecule. Step 2: The breakdown of the fuel generates NADH, as a pair of high-energy electrons are stripped from acetic acid and added to NAD plus (forming NADH). Step 3: Acetic acid attaches to coenzyme A. Output (which goes to the citric acid cycle): Acetyl C O A, a two-carbon molecule attached to coenzyme A.

The Citric Acid Cycle

Text description of this image

The details of the input, steps, and output depicted in the figure are as follows: Input: Step 1: 2-carbon acetic acid. It joins a four-carbon acceptor molecule, becoming 6-carbon citric acid, and enters the citric acid cycle. Output: Step 2: 2 C O2 (each C O2 contains one carbon atom) An input of ADP plus phosphate to the citric acid cycle results in an output of ATP in step 3. An input of 3 NAD plus to the citric acid cycle results in step 4 which is shown as an output of 3 NADH (each NADH carries a pair of high-energy electrons) An input of FAD to the citric acid cycle results in step 5 which is shown as an output of one FADH2 (which carries a pair of high-energy electrons) Step 6: The four-carbon acceptor molecule is recycled to be used again in the citric acid cycle.

Electron Transport Chain

  • During cellular respiration, the electrons gathered from food molecules gradually “fall,” losing energy at each step.
    • Electrons are transferred from glucose in food molecules to NAD+.
    • This electron transfer converts NAD+ to NADH.
    • Then NADH releases two electrons that enter an electron transport chain, a series of electron carrier molecules. With each exchange, the electron gives up a bit of energy.
Text description of this image

A worker wearing a hard hat uses a glucose hammer to strike a lever which sends an electron from the ground level to the top of a tower which is 3 platforms high.; Another worker catches the electron at the top of the tower and puts it on the mill conveyor labeled electron transport chain flowing down to the first platform of the tower.; As the electron travels down the conveyor, ATP is produced and released.

Where are the electrons going?

The overall effect of all this transfer of electrons during cellular respiration is a “downward” trip for electrons

  • from glucose,
  • to NADH,
  • to an electron transport chain, and
  • to oxygen.

The Role of Oxygen in Harvesting Food Energy

Text description of this image

A pair of electrons from food are transferred to NAD plus, forming NADH. NADH transfers those electrons to the electron transport chain, reforming NAD plus. The two electrons fall in small steps down the electron transport chain toward oxygen, releasing energy at each step. This stepwise release of energy is used to make ATP. At the bottom of the electron transport chain, two electrons plus half a molecule of O2 plus 2 hydrogen ions combine to form water (H2O).

The Mitochondrion: Site of Cellular Respiration

Text description of this image

An image and a transmission electron micrograph at a magnification of 50,000 of the mitochondrion, show an outer membrane and an inner membrane with space between them. Many infoldings called cristae can be seen in the matrix enclosed in the membranes.

Text description of this image

The details of various steps shown in the figure are as follows: Steps 1: In the mitochondrial matrix, NADH transfers two electrons to the first protein complex (electron carrier), forming NAD plus. Step 2: FADH2 transfers its pair of electrons to the next protein complex in the chain, forming FAD. Step 3: The transfer of these electrons causes hydrogen ion to be pumped through the protein complexes in the electron transport chain from the mitochondrial matrix across the inner membrane to the space between membranes. Step 4: Oxygen pulls the electrons down the chain; with a pair of electrons half a molecule of O2 plus 2 hydrogen ions go to H2O. Step 5:: Electron pumping during the electron transport chain creates a concentration gradient of hydrogen ions, where there is a high concentration of hydrogen ions in the space between membranes relative to the mitochondrial matrix. The hydrogen ions rush down the concentration gradient through the ATP synthase, an enzyme also embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane. ATP synthase spins as hydrogen ions fall through it toward the matrix. Step 6: The spinning ATP synthase adds a phosphate to ADP, forming ATP. A skull and crossbones are drawn beside the final protein complex in the electron transport chain.

Summary of Cellular Respiration

Text description of this image

The summary of ATP yield during cellular respiration shown in the diagram is as follows: Stage 1: Glycolysis: Glucose goes to two molecules of pyruvic acid.

ATP is formed by direct synthesis and it takes place in the cytoplasm. 2 NADH are also formed during this step and each carries a pair of electrons to the electron transport chain.; Net ATP: 2

Stage 2: Two molecules of pyruvic acid from glycolysis enter the mitochondrion and are converted to 2 acetyl coenzyme A molecules, which enters the citric acid cycle. 2 molecules of NADH are also formed and each carries a pair of electrons to the electron transport chain.

Net ATP: 0

Stage 3: Citric Acid Cycle

ATP is formed by direct synthesis; takes place in the mitochondrion. 6 NADH and 2 FADH2 are also formed during this step; each will carry a pair of electrons to the electron transport chain.; Net ATP: 2

Stage 4: Electron Transport Chain

ATP is formed by the ATP synthase; takes place in the mitochondrion.; Net ATP: About 28

The maximum number of ATP formed per molecule of glucose is about 32.

Energy From Food

Text description of this image

Food is broken down into carbohydrates, fats, and proteins. These are broken down into monomers that are shown entering cellular respiration as fuel at different stages. The stages of cellular respiration are shown in order: Glycolysis, Acetyl C o A (not a stage, but links glycolysis and the citric acid cycle), the citric acid cycle, and the electron transport chain. Glycolysis, the citric acid cycle, and the electron transport chain are shown producing ATP.he details of where the monomers enter cellular respiration follows: 1. Carbohydrates are broken down into sugars which are shown entering glycolysis. 2. Fats are broken down into glycerol and fatty acids. Glycerol is shown entering glycolysis. Fatty acids are shown entering to produce acetyl C o A. 3. Proteins are broken into amino acids which are shown entering glycolysis, to produce acetyl C o A, and the citric acid cycle.

Fermentation: Anaerobic Harvest of Food Energy

  • Some of your cells can work for short periods without oxygen. This anaerobic (“without oxygen”) harvest of food energy is called fermentation.
  • Fermentation relies on glycolysis, the first stage of cellular respiration.
  • Glycolysis does not require O2 but does produce two ATP molecules for each glucose molecule broken down to pyruvic acid.

Fermentation

Alcoholic Fermentation

Lactic Acid Fermentation

Text description of this image

Input: One six-carbon molecule of glucose.; Glucose is split during glycolysis into two 3-carbon molecules of pyruvic acid. In the process, 2 ADP plus 2 phosphates go to 2 ATP and 2 NAD plus accept a pair of electrons each to form 2 NADH.; The two 3-carbon molecules of pyruvic acid then go to 2 molecules of 2-carbon ethyl alcohol as 2 molecules of C O 2 are released and 2 NADH plus 2 hydrogen ions go to 2 NAD plus. The NAD plus are recycled to accept electrons again during glycolysis.; Output: Two 2-carbon ethyl alcohol molecules.

Text description of this image

Input: Glucose, a 6-carbon molecule.; Glucose is split during glycolysis into two 3-carbon molecules of pyruvic acid. In the process, 2 ADP plus 2 phosphates go to 2 ATP and 2 NAD plus accept a pair of electrons each to form 2 NADH. Next, the two NADH plus 2 hydrogen ions go to 2 NAD plus, which are recycled back to the first step to receive electrons during glycolysis.; Output: Two 3-carbon molecules of lactic acid.

Timeline of Oxygen and Life on Earth

Text description of this image

The details of the timeline are as follows:

Origin of Earth occurred over 4.5 billions of years ago; Oldest prokaryotic fossils appeared about 3.5 billions of years ago; Atmospheric oxygen first appeared about 2.7 billions of years ago; Atmospheric oxygen reached 10 percent of modern levels about 2.2 billions of years ago; First eukaryotic organisms appeared about 2.1 billions of years ago; The atmospheric oxygen at modern levels is depicted near the present, at zero billions of years ago, in the timeline.
